title: Climbing Lobuche Peak: Full Guide
excerpt: Lobuche Peak, 6,119 m, is a technical summit above the Khumbu Glacier. The full guide: the route via Everest Base Camp, acclimatization, high camp, summit day, gear, permits and cost.
seoTitle: Climbing Lobuche East: Route, Gear, Permit and Cost

content.value: In the small hours of the night, in the tents of high camp at 5,300 m, climbers switch on their headlamps and set out for the summit of Lobuche, 6,119 m (20,075 ft). Lobuche Peak, in full Lobuche East, is a summit in the Khumbu region of eastern Nepal, above the village of Lobuche and opposite the Khumbu Glacier, and from its top Everest stands close at hand. It requires high physical fitness, technical climbing skills and previous experience on high-altitude routes, and its summit day crosses rock, snow and ice, with crampons, an ice axe and a jumar on fixed ropes. The climbing seasons are spring and fall, and with us it is a 19-day expedition that also takes in Everest Base Camp and Kala Patthar on the way.

Lobuche is a peak for people who have already walked at altitude and want to take the step into real mountaineering. Up to the village of Lobuche it is a trek on trails with nights in teahouses, and from there the harness, the helmet and the ropes begin. Here is what you need to know before you decide: which summit this actually is, how our route works day by day, why the trek to Everest Base Camp is part of the acclimatization, what happens on summit day, which gear and training you need, how you reach Lukla and what the price includes.
Lobuche East, the summit above the trail

Lobuche has two summits joined by a single ridge. Lobuche East, 6,119 m, is the summit that expeditions climb on a climbing permit from the Nepal Mountaineering Association, and it is the one our expedition goes to. Lobuche West, 6,145 m, is considered an expedition peak and requires a different permit. When people talk about Lobuche Peak, they usually mean the eastern summit.

The mountain rises above the village of Lobuche, 4,940 m, within Sagarmatha National Park. It sits very close to the Everest Base Camp trail, so it fits into it naturally: you go up to Base Camp and Kala Patthar, return to Lobuche, and turn from there toward the mountain. From the summit you look out over Everest, Lhotse, Nuptse and Ama Dablam, and over the Khumbu Icefall, the first section of the route to the summit of Everest from the Nepal side.

The peak also has a role in the world of the big expeditions: climbers preparing for summits above 8,000 m climb it to adapt to altitude. For those who come to it as a first peak, it offers real technical climbing, with a helmet, harness, ice axe, jumar and crampons on snow, ice and rock, without especially extreme technical challenges. Technically the route is of moderate difficulty, and we grade the expedition as a whole, with its altitude and long days, as challenging.

content.value: Our route, day by day
The HighAir Lobuche Peak expedition lasts 19 days, from arrival in Kathmandu to departure. The altitudes in brackets are those of the overnight stop or of the high point of that day:

items: Day 1: arrival in Kathmandu and transfer to the hotel.
Day 2: preparation day in Kathmandu and a gear check.
Day 3: flight to Lukla and a walk to Phakding (2,610 m).
Day 4: up to Namche Bazaar (3,440 m).
Day 5: acclimatization day in Namche Bazaar.
Day 10: Everest Base Camp (5,364 m) and down to sleep at Gorak Shep (5,140 m).
Day 11: climb to Kala Patthar (5,545 m) and back to Lobuche (4,940 m).
Day 12: up from Lobuche to Lobuche Peak High Camp (5,300 m).
Day 13: summit day (6,119 m) and down to Thukla (4,620 m).
Day 16: the last walking day, to Lukla (2,860 m).
Day 17: flight from Lukla to Kathmandu or Ramechhap.
Day 18: spare day in case of bad weather, or a free day in Kathmandu.
Day 19: transfer to the airport and flight home.

content.value: The itinerary is built in two stages. In the first you walk the classic Khumbu valley trail to Everest Base Camp and climb Kala Patthar. In the second you return to the village of Lobuche and climb from it toward the mountain. The order is deliberate: by the time you set out for the summit, your body has already spent more than a week at altitude.

content.title: ✦ The trek is the acclimatization
content.value: By the time you reach Lobuche Peak High Camp, 5,300 m, you have already slept a night at Gorak Shep, 5,140 m, and stood on Kala Patthar, 5,545 m. The trek to Everest Base Camp is part of the acclimatization for the summit.
On the way: the Khumbu valley and Everest Base Camp

From Lukla, 2,860 m, you walk up the Dudh Koshi river valley to Namche Bazaar, the Sherpa market town, and continue through Tengboche and its monastery and through Dingboche to the village of Lobuche, and from there to Gorak Shep and Base Camp. On the way there are two acclimatization days, in Namche Bazaar and Dingboche, on which you sleep at the same altitude as the night before.

Throughout the trek you sleep in teahouses, the simple lodges of Nepal, in twin rooms, and three meals a day, chosen from the menu, are included in the price. Every climber has a personal porter who carries up to 25 kg, and you walk with a daypack. Internet, laundry and extra meals at the teahouses are not included, so bring some cash for them.
Up to day 10 the walking route is identical to our Everest Base Camp trek, and we have written a complete guide to it, describing each section and life in the teahouses.

content.value: Acclimatization: altitude sets the pace

The main risk on Lobuche is not only the technical climbing but the altitude. The higher you go, the less oxygen each breath brings in, and the body needs time to adapt. The accepted rule in mountain medicine is that above 3,000 m you do not raise your sleeping altitude by more than 500 m a night, and you add a night of acclimatization for every 1,000 m of sleeping altitude gained. For some climbers even this pace is too fast, so listen to your body.

Altitude sickness usually starts with a headache, sometimes joined by loss of appetite, dizziness, fatigue and nausea. When symptoms get worse despite rest at the same altitude, you descend. With us the decision to continue always belongs to the guide, and safety comes before the summit. Every group carries a pulse oximeter and a Magnus satellite device, and we keep close watch on how everyone adapts to altitude all the way.

The itinerary is built around this principle: two acclimatization days on the way in, a night at Gorak Shep and a climb of Kala Patthar before you reach the mountain, and after the summit a descent the same day to Thukla, 4,620 m, 680 m lower than high camp. In the mountains there is no promise of reaching the summit, but there is always a commitment to safety above all.
Lobuche village and high camp

On day 11, after the climb to Kala Patthar, you return to the village of Lobuche, 4,940 m, for a last night in a teahouse before the mountain. Some expeditions set up a tented base camp at the foot of the mountain. Our itinerary has no such night: the night before the climb to high camp is spent in a teahouse in the village.

On day 12 you climb from Lobuche to high camp, 5,300 m, a gain of about 360 meters. There you sleep in HighAir twin tents, and it is the only night of the expedition not spent in a teahouse or a hotel. The relatively short climb lets you reach camp rested, sort your gear for the night and get to sleep early, because the start for the summit comes well before dawn.
Summit day
At night, on the rock slabs

Summit day starts in the small hours of the night, on most expeditions at around 2 a.m., so that there is time to go up and come down while the snow is still firm. The first hours pass by headlamp, on rock slabs that steepen gradually. When the rock is covered in ice or snow, walking on it calls for care, and sometimes you rope up already on this section. At the top of the rock, at a spot known as crampon point, you put on crampons and move onto snow and ice.
Snow, ice and fixed ropes

Above crampon point you climb steep slopes of snow and ice, and on the steepest sections you move on fixed ropes. You climb them with a jumar, an ascender that locks onto the rope and is attached to your harness: you slide it up, take a step in your crampons and lean on it when needed. At each anchor you move from one rope to the next, always clipped in. The upper part follows a snow ridge to the summit, 6,119 m. At this altitude every step takes several breaths, and the condition of the snow and ice changes from season to season.
The descent, down to Thukla

The steep sections are usually descended on the fixed ropes, rappelling with a descender attached to the harness. You return to high camp, pack it up and continue the same day to Thukla, 4,620 m, where a teahouse waits. With us summit day lasts 10 to 12 hours, and it is the longest and most demanding day of the expedition.

content.title: ✦ Summit day in numbers
content.value: A start in the small hours of the night from high camp, 5,300 m. A climb of 819 m to the summit, 6,119 m, and a descent of 1,499 m to Thukla, 4,620 m. In total 10 to 12 hours.
Technical gear and training

On Lobuche you use professional climbing gear: a helmet, harness, ice axe, jumar, crampons and fixed ropes, on the snow, ice and rock of the mountain. Before summit day participants are trained on this gear, including ascending a fixed rope with a jumar, and a descender is usually used for going down the rope. On summit day every climber has a personal climbing guide. If you have never used a jumar or rappelled, you will gain a great deal from practice at a climbing gym or a short course near home before departure, so that on the mountain the movements already feel familiar in your hands.

Personal gear, meaning clothing, footwear and climbing equipment, is not included in the price, and a full gear list is sent to every registrant after registration. A climbing gear rental kit is available for 300 dollars. The most important item is a pair of high-altitude mountaineering boots that take crampons and keep your feet warm in the cold of the night. Before departure you receive a personal gear checklist and an online gear consultation, and the group meets the guide on an online preparation call.
The flight to Lukla

The expedition starts and ends in Lukla, the village that is home to the airport of the Everest region. In our package the flights to Lukla and back are by plane, and they are included in the price. Lukla airport is considered one of the most challenging in the world because of its short runway, and flights stop whenever the weather does not allow them. Cloud and fog can stop them for several days in a row.

In the busy seasons most flights to Lukla leave from the airport at Manthali in Ramechhap district, a few hours' drive from Kathmandu, not from Kathmandu itself. In our itinerary the return flight from Lukla lands in Kathmandu or Ramechhap. If you prefer, you can fly Kathmandu–Lukla–Kathmandu by helicopter for an extra 800 dollars per person. Day 18 is a spare day in Kathmandu in case the flight from Lukla is delayed, and if it is not needed it becomes a free day in the city.
Permits, visa and insurance

To enter the area you need two permits: the Sagarmatha National Park entry permit and the entry permit of the local authority, Khumbu Pasang Lhamu Rural Municipality. The climb itself also requires a climbing permit from the Nepal Mountaineering Association. The permit price depends on the season, and it is lower in the fall than in spring. Both entry permits and the Lobuche Peak climbing permit are included in the price of our expedition.

Most visitors, including UK, EU, US, Canadian and Australian citizens, get a Nepal tourist visa on arrival at Kathmandu airport or apply online in advance. For a 19-day trip you need the 30-day visa, which costs 50 US dollars (as of 2026) and is not included. Travel and medical insurance is not included either. Before buying a policy, check that it covers climbing up to 6,119 m, including rescue and helicopter evacuation, and check your government's current travel advice for Nepal before you go.
When to go

Nepal has two main climbing seasons: spring, before the monsoon, and fall, after it. Our Lobuche Peak expeditions depart in April and May, and in September and October. In the fall, once the rains are over, the air is usually clear and the views open, but the nights at altitude are cold. In spring the days are warmer on the lower part of the route, and clouds sometimes build in the afternoon. In the monsoon months, in summer, rain and cloud disrupt the flights to Lukla, and in winter the cold at altitude is very harsh.
Lobuche, Island Peak or Mera Peak

We grade our three expeditions to summits above 6,000 m in Nepal as challenging, but each is a different way to a summit. Mera Peak, 6,476 m, is the highest and least technical of the three: walking on glaciers and snow with some steep sections, with no previous climbing experience required, on a 19-day route through the Hinku valley. Island Peak, 6,189 m, is a 20-day expedition that passes Everest Base Camp and turns toward Chhukung, and on the way to the summit you cross snow and a glacier and climb fixed ropes with a jumar. Lobuche, 6,119 m, is the lowest of the three, but climbing it requires technical climbing skills, and it is the closest to the Base Camp trail.

content.value: Who it suits

Lobuche Peak suits anyone who wants a first Himalayan summit with real technical climbing, and anyone who plans to go on to higher peaks in the future and wants to gain experience with climbing gear on snow, ice and rock. The climb requires high physical fitness, technical climbing skills and previous experience on high-altitude routes, but it does not involve especially extreme technical challenges. In terms of fitness, you need to be able to walk about 20 km a day and to handle a summit day of 10 to 12 hours.

A medical certificate and a health declaration are conditions for departure, and anyone who does not meet the health or physical requirements will not be able to join. The best preparation is long uphill hikes with a pack on your back in the months before departure, together with practice on ropes if you have no experience with them.

Good to know: the climb is led by experienced local Sherpa guides who speak English and have long experience leading groups in the mountains. Basic English, enough to follow instructions on the ground, including on the ropes, is worth having. Following the instructions of the crew is mandatory, and the route may change with the weather and at the discretion of the guides.
What it costs and what is included

The Lobuche Peak expedition costs 3,900 US dollars per person. It includes airport transfers to the hotel in Kathmandu and back, internal transfers to the start of the route and back, domestic flights to Lukla and back, 3 nights in a 5-star hotel in Kathmandu in a single room with breakfast, teahouse accommodation in shared rooms throughout the trek, double tents during the climb, dinners at a restaurant before and after the climb, full service at high camp with cooking gear and food for the altitude, three full meals a day throughout the climb, 2 liters of hot water a day, professional local English-speaking guides, a personal climbing guide for every climber on summit day, porters for personal gear up to 25 kg per person, showers and toilets in the teahouses where available on the route, all entry permits for the trek and the climb, a first aid kit with emergency oxygen cylinders, a pulse oximeter for the group, a Magnus satellite device for the group, a personal area in the HighAir app, a detailed gear list and a training plan for the climb, an online gear consultation, an online preparation call with your group and guide before departure, support with flight and travel insurance questions before departure, a gift kit with a cap, a dry-fit shirt and a 100-liter duffel bag, and a meaningful donation to the fight against cancer.

Not included: international flights, travel and medical insurance with evacuation cover (required), lunch and dinner at the hotel in Kathmandu, personal gear (clothing, footwear, climbing gear and summit boots), tips for guides and porters (250 dollars per person), a summit bonus for the guides (250 dollars per person), the Nepal visa (50 dollars), an extra hotel night if needed, vaccinations and travel clinic advice, and personal expenses such as drinks, alcohol, laundry, gifts and internet. At extra cost you can add a climbing gear rental kit (300 dollars per person), helicopter flights from Kathmandu to Lukla and back (800 dollars per person), or a single room in the teahouses (20 dollars a night).
Note that in the event of an early descent from the mountain, for any reason, the additional costs, such as extra hotel nights, meals and flight changes, are borne by the climber.
Lobuche Peak with HighAir

At HighAir we go to Lobuche Peak in spring and fall, in groups of up to 10 participants, and the success rate we publish on the mountain is 82 percent. Our itinerary is built so that the trek to Everest Base Camp serves as acclimatization for the summit: two acclimatization days, a night at Gorak Shep and a climb of Kala Patthar before you reach the mountain, and a spare day at the end.

A portion of the proceeds from every expedition we run is dedicated to supporting cancer patients, because the mountains, in our view, are also a way of giving back. Every climber you see on the summits of the world started once, on one mountain. If Lobuche is your first technical summit in the Himalaya, we are here.
Frequently asked questions
How many days does a Lobuche Peak climb take?

The HighAir expedition lasts 19 days, from arrival in Kathmandu to departure. 14 of them are spent between landing in Lukla and getting back there, including the trek to Everest Base Camp and Kala Patthar, two acclimatization days, a night at high camp and summit day. There is also a preparation day in Kathmandu and a spare day in case of bad weather.
Do you need climbing experience to climb Lobuche Peak?

The climb requires high physical fitness, technical climbing skills and previous experience on high-altitude routes, but it does not involve especially extreme technical challenges. On summit day you use a helmet, harness, ice axe, crampons and a jumar on fixed ropes, and before summit day participants are trained on the gear. A medical certificate and a health declaration are also required.
How much does it cost to climb Lobuche Peak?

The HighAir expedition costs 3,900 US dollars per person, and the price includes the flights to Lukla, accommodation, meals along the trek, the guides, porters, entry permits and the climbing permit. Not included are international flights, insurance, personal and climbing gear, the Nepal visa (50 dollars), tips (250 dollars) and a summit bonus for the guides (250 dollars).
When is the season to climb Lobuche Peak?

Spring and fall, before and after the monsoon. Our expeditions depart in April and May, and in September and October. In the fall the air is usually clear and the nights cold, while in spring the days are warmer and clouds sometimes build in the afternoon.
What is the difference between Lobuche East and Lobuche West?

Lobuche East, 6,119 m, is the summit that expeditions climb on a climbing permit from the Nepal Mountaineering Association, and it is the one our expedition goes to. Lobuche West, 6,145 m, is a separate summit on the same ridge, considered an expedition peak and requiring a different permit. When people talk about Lobuche Peak, they usually mean the eastern summit.
What language do the guides speak?
The climb is led by experienced local Sherpa guides who speak English and have long experience leading groups in the mountains.
